content.title: About
content.content: Dulce de leche is a sweet caramelized milk paste made by slowly heating milk with sugar until the mixture thickens and turns a golden‑brown color. It has a smooth, creamy flavor with notes of caramel and vanilla.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A traditional dessert throughout Latin America, especially in Argentina, Uruguay and Peru.
The name “dulce de leche” translates to “sweet from milk”.
In some regions it is called “cajeta” (Mexico) or “manjar blanco” (Chile).
Originally prepared in large copper cauldrons over open fire.
Many variations exist, adding vanilla, coconut, chocolate or nuts.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The milk base provides a notable amount of calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Milk protein helps maintain muscle tissue.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Heat‑processed milk retains vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: High carbohydrate content quickly replenishes glycogen stores.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Caramelization creates melanoidins that have antioxidant properties.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large servings can raise blood glucose levels and contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance should limit intake or choose lactose‑free versions.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic individuals may react to casein and whey proteins.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One tablespoon provides about 60–70 kcal; moderation is key.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use dulce de leche as a filling for crepes, cakes, ice cream, swirl into yogurt, spread on toast, stir into coffee, or simply enjoy a spoonful as a dessert. It can be melted into sauces or batter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight jar in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 weeks. For longer keeping, freeze in small portions; thaw in the fridge before use.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-tomatoe.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with tomatoes, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with tomatoes is a dish made from eggs cooked together with diced tomatoes and a small amount of fat (oil, butter, or other cooking fat). Eggs provide a complete set of proteins, while tomatoes add vitamin C, lycopene, and fresh flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes cooked with eggs increase lycopene absorption thanks to the added fat.
Eggs contain all essential amino acids, making them a high‑quality protein source.
The dish can be prepared in under 10 minutes.
Around the world, variations include different herbs and spices, but the basic recipe stays the same.
The combination of eggs and tomatoes may boost mood due to tryptophan content.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs supply high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin D and B12
items.content: Eggs are one of the few natural foods providing vitamin D and vitamin B12, important for bone health and nervous system function.

items.title: Lycopene from tomatoes
items.content: Lycopene is a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: A modest amount of cooking oil adds monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids needed for overall health.

items.title: Eye health support
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in the yolk help protect eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg proteins.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume in moderation.

items.title: Excessive fat
items.content: Using too much oil can increase calorie count and lead to formation of unhealthy trans fats.

items.title: Salt and seasoning
items.content: Over‑salting adds strain to kidneys and the cardiovascular system.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat the eggs, stir in diced tomatoes and a pinch of salt. Heat a pan, melt a small amount of oil, pour in the egg mixture and stir gently until the desired consistency is reached. Optional additions include herbs, cheese, or spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a pan or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus) is an edible pod widely used in African, Asian, and Southern U.S. cuisines. When cooked, the pods become tender while retaining a light mucilaginous texture and a mild flavor. Okra is rich in vitamins, minerals, and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Okra is sometimes called “gumbo” because of its characteristic slimy texture after cooking.
In the United States, fried okra is popular in the South, but boiled okra is commonly used in soups and stews.
Okra seeds can be pressed to produce oil that is high in linoleic acid.
The plant thrives in warm climates and can grow up to 2 meters tall.
Traditional medicine in some cultures uses okra pods to relieve constipation and aid digestion.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cooked okra provides a good amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K and folate
items.content: These nutrients are important for blood clotting and cell health, especially during pregnancy.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, helps regulate blood sugar levels, and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Minerals: potassium, magnesium, calcium
items.content: Potassium aids fluid balance, magnesium supports muscle and nerve function, and calcium is essential for bone health.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A 100 g serving of boiled okra contains about 30 kcal, making it a suitable choice for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to okra, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Raw pods contain oxalates that can cause gastrointestinal discomfort; cooking neutralizes them.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: High potassium levels may enhance the effects of blood‑pressure‑lowering drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boiled okra is used in soups, stews, vegetable casseroles, and salads. It can be added to curries, couscous, or rice dishes. For a softer texture, soak the pods in cold water before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh okra pods in the refrigerator in a bag or container, where they stay crisp for up to 5 days. Cooked okra should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 3‑4 days.

spinach-canned-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Spinach, canned, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Canned spinach is cooked spinach leaves packed in a sealed jar without added fat. The product retains most of its nutrients, a mild flavor, and a bright green color. It is commonly used as a ready‑to‑use ingredient in soups, side dishes, and casseroles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach is one of the richest plant sources of iron and vitamin K.
Canning allows spinach to be stored for 2‑3 years while preserving key nutrients.
In the United States, canned spinach is a staple for dishes like spinach dip and baked casseroles.
Spinach belongs to the Amaranth family and grows in temperate climates.
Without added fat, canned spinach is low in calories – about 20 kcal per 100 g.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Good source of iron
items.content: Iron supports hemoglobin formation and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Suitable for weight‑management diets due to its low fat and calorie content.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber in spinach promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Canned versions can contain added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to spinach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned spinach can be stirred into soups, sauces, omelets, casseroles, or used as a base for dips. Shake the jar well before use, and optionally drain excess liquid.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened jar in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep it in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Tortilla chips are crisp slices made from corn tortillas, prepared with reduced fat and without added salt. They have a light, slightly sweet corn flavor and work well as a snack on their own or as a base for various dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tortilla chips originated in Mexico as a way to use leftover tortilla dough.
Low‑fat versions are often baked instead of fried.
The lack of salt makes them suitable for low‑sodium diets.
Corn, the main ingredient, is rich in antioxidants such as lutein and zeaxanthin.
Tortilla chips are commonly served with nachos, guacamole, and salsa.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Reduced‑fat chips contain fewer calories than traditional fried versions, helping with energy balance.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Corn tortillas provide a steady release of energy, supporting stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Corn fiber aids digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin help protect eye health.

items.title: No added salt
items.content: The absence of salt benefits people with hypertension or those monitoring sodium intake.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to corn, experiencing skin or respiratory reactions.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Certain brands add wheat flour; check the label if you need a gluten‑free product.

items.title: Loss of crunch if stored improperly
items.content: Moisture can soften the chips; keep them in an airtight container.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy tortilla chips as a standalone snack, with guacamole, salsa, hummus, or as a base for nachos. They also add a pleasant crunch to salads and soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store chips in a tightly sealed bag or container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to maintain crispness.
